clue.text: Now would I give a thousand —— of sea for an of barren ground" (The Tempest)

definitions.text: Now would I give a thousand —— of sea for an of barren ground" (The Tempest)

parts.words: Now would I give a thousand —— of sea for an of barren ground" (The Tempest)
parts.note: a quotation to complete: Gonzalo, fearing shipwreck in the opening scene of The Tempest, would trade a great stretch of sea, measured in eighths of a mile, for a patch of dry land

explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue has dropped a word: Gonzalo's line reads 'for an acre of barren ground'. The missing unit is a racing measure of an eighth of a mile.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap needs a plural unit of distance, an eighth of a mile each, set against the acre of land in the same line.

clue.text: Unit associated with fortune by Dame Ivy Compton-Burnett

definitions.meaning: a household group, the basic social unit

definitions.text: associated with fortune by Dame Ivy Compton-Burnett
definitions.meaning: Compton-Burnett's 1939 novel is titled A ____ and a Fortune

explanation.surface: A grouping linked to wealth in an English novelist's work.
explanation.definitionFit: Parents and children form the basic social unit, and the word partners 'Fortune' in Compton-Burnett's title.

clue.text: "Race-horse sired, not —— born" (Browning)

parts.note: a quotation to complete: Browning contrasts a thoroughbred father with a humbler mother, an ordinary riding horse

explanation.walkthrough: The gap needs an archaic word for a common saddle horse, the opposite of a race-horse; Chaucer's Shipman rides one.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for an ordinary riding horse or nag, set against the thoroughbred sire.

clue.text: He created a storm in Russian theatre

definitions.text: He created a storm in Russian theatre

parts.words: He created a storm in Russian theatre
parts.note: reads as causing an uproar, but means writing the play The Storm, a classic of Russian drama

explanation.walkthrough: 'Created a storm' suggests a scandal; it is literal, as the 1859 play is titled The Storm.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander Ostrovsky was the Russian dramatist who wrote The Storm.

clue.text: Equable, not quite like Bach's keyboard

definitions.meaning: Bach's collection is The Well-Tempered Clavier, so swap 'well' for its near-synonym 'good'

explanation.surface: Calm in temperament, unlike the tuning of Bach's instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: Bach's keyboard is 'well' tempered; 'not quite' points to the nearly equivalent 'good'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone even-natured and calm is equable.

clue.text: "Ask me no more where Jove ——s, / When June is past, the fading rose" (Thomas Carew)

definitions.text: "Ask me no more where Jove ——s, / When June is past, the fading rose" (Thomas Carew)

parts.words: "Ask me no more where Jove ——s, / When June is past, the fading rose" (Thomas Carew)
parts.note: a quotation to complete: the opening of Carew's song asks where the god places or gives away the fading summer rose

explanation.walkthrough: The verb missing from Carew's opening line means gives or places; the printed 's' after the gap makes it third person.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap needs a verb meaning to give or confer, as Jove disposes of the faded rose.

clue.text: Huge part of Italian tenor might overwhelm opera

indicators.note: only a part of the following words supplies the letters, a run inside them

explanation.surface: The great voice of an Italian tenor could drown out an opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Enorm is an archaic word for enormous, vast.

clue.text: Brecht's coach

parts.note: Brecht adapted Lenz's play Der Hofmeister, whose title means a private teacher

explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' suggests a vehicle, but it means a private teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: A coach is a private teacher, and Brecht's adaptation of Lenz bears that title.

clue.text: One observer at Selborne for type of pochard?

parts.note: Gilbert White was the naturalist of Selborne
an eye is one organ that observes

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher in a Hampshire village spotting a kind of duck.
explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert White wrote The Natural History of Selborne, about that Hampshire village; the question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: The white-eye, or ferruginous duck, is a diving duck of the pochard group.

clue.text: Great pleasure following steed of a French herald

indicators.note: the great pleasure comes after the steed, so its word is placed second

parts.note: a steed is a horse you ride, a mount
great pleasure is joy

explanation.surface: A French herald's delight on getting his horse.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Henry V, Montjoy is the French herald who carries messages to King Henry.
explanation.definitionFit: A named character: the herald of the French king in Henry V.

clue.text: Senior version of cloth of gold

indicators.note: a new version of a word gives its letters in a fresh order

explanation.surface: An older form of some luxurious gilded fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Soneri is an Indian term for a rich gold-threaded fabric.

clue.text: Shakespeare's epiphany?

parts.note: reads as a sudden insight of the playwright, but means his comedy named for the evening of the feast of the Epiphany

explanation.walkthrough: 'Epiphany' suggests a revelation; here it is the church feast on 6 January, and Shakespeare's comedy is named for its eve.
explanation.definitionFit: The feast falls twelve days after Christmas, giving the title of Shakespeare's comedy.

clue.text: A fantastic part in Shakespearean problem play

definitions.text: A fantastic part in Shakespearean problem play

parts.words: A fantastic part in Shakespearean problem play
parts.note: the cast list of Measure for Measure, one of Shakespeare's problem plays, describes one character simply as 'a fantastic', meaning a fanciful dandy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fantastic' looks like praise, but it is the old noun for a showy, whimsical fellow, which is exactly how the dramatis personae label this role.
explanation.definitionFit: The play's own list of characters names this role as 'a fantastic'.

clue.text: Beatrix Potter's Johnny

parts.note: Beatrix Potter wrote The Tale of Johnny ..., about a city rodent and his country cousin

explanation.definitionFit: The full name of Potter's character, the city-dwelling cousin of Timmy Willie.

clue.text: Straightforward yarn by the playwright of Mansfield Park

definitions.text: by the playwright of Mansfield Park
definitions.meaning: Elizabeth Inchbald wrote Lovers' Vows, the play rehearsed in Mansfield Park, and also this 1791 novel

explanation.surface: An uncomplicated tale written by the dramatist behind Austen's amateur theatricals.
explanation.walkthrough: Mansfield Park has no playwright of its own; the reference is to Inchbald, whose play the Bertram household stages in Austen's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally an uncomplicated tale, and also the title of Inchbald's novel.

clue.text: Low Countries organist hammered out new sickle

indicators.note: hammered out means beaten into a new shape, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A Dutch musician beating a fresh blade into shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Jan Pieterszoon Sweelinck was a Dutch organist and composer of Amsterdam.

clue.text: French composer rhapsodized in Spain

parts.note: the composer wrote España, an orchestral rhapsody inspired by his travels in Spain

explanation.definitionFit: Emmanuel Chabrier was the French composer of the rhapsody España.

clue.text: Feline city not applicable for Highland heroine

parts.note: a feline is a cat
Rio de Janeiro, a city

explanation.surface: A cat from a city, irrelevant to a Scottish heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Catriona is the title heroine of Stevenson's sequel to Kidnapped, set in the Scottish Highlands.

clue.text: A rough time for the Empress of Blandings

definitions.meaning: an idiom for a difficult passage, as in making hard work of something
the Empress of Blandings is Lord Emsworth's prize pig in P. G. Wodehouse, who features in his 1933 novel of this title

explanation.surface: Trouble ahead for Lord Emsworth's prize sow.
explanation.walkthrough: The Empress sounds like royalty but is a pig; she appears in the Wodehouse Blandings novel with this title.
explanation.definitionFit: Making heavy going of things is an idiom for struggle, and it is also the title of a Blandings novel.

clue.text: Unconventional poetess upsets posh pa

indicators.note: upsets means knocks over, throwing the letters into disorder

explanation.surface: A bohemian woman poet scandalises her snobbish father.
explanation.definitionFit: Sappho of Lesbos, the Greek lyric poet, whose life defied convention.

clue.text: A. S. Byatt's eponymous creature in dissenting body

parts.note: a sect is a breakaway religious group

explanation.surface: A Byatt title creature found in a nonconformist group.
explanation.walkthrough: Byatt's novella collection is Angels and Insects, so the creature names the book.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the two kinds of being in the title of Byatt's Angels and Insects.

clue.text: Best inner arrangement for conductor

indicators.note: an arrangement of the words gives their letters in a new order, fitting the musical setting

explanation.surface: The finest internal orchestration for the man with the baton.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonard Bernstein was an American conductor and composer.

clue.text: Strange, Keats as Victorian literary scholar and editor

indicators.note: strange signals the poet's name is made odd, its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: Oddly, a Romantic poet turns into a Victorian philologist.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter William Skeat was a Victorian philologist who edited Chaucer and Piers Plowman.

clue.text: Acquire knowledge of king and knight

parts.note: Lear is Shakespeare's king
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: Getting to know a monarch and one of his knights.
explanation.definitionFit: To come to know something through study is a synonym for acquiring knowledge.

clue.text: Posthumus marriage created difficulties for her

definitions.text: Posthumus marriage created difficulties for her

parts.words: Posthumus marriage created difficulties for her
parts.note: in Cymbeline, the king's daughter secretly weds Posthumus Leonatus, which brings banishment and trials upon her

explanation.walkthrough: 'Posthumus' looks like 'after death', but it is the name of the hero of Cymbeline.
explanation.definitionFit: She is Cymbeline's daughter, whose secret union with Posthumus drives the play's troubles.

clue.text: Gap Paine possibly created in sacred source

indicators.note: possibly signals the words could be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: A gap Tom Paine might have made in a holy spring.
explanation.definitionFit: Aganippe is the spring on Mount Helicon sacred to the Muses, a fount of poetic inspiration.

clue.text: Rhode Island counter-tenor on bridge

parts.note: RI is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Rhode Island
an alto is a high male voice, a counter-tenor

explanation.surface: A singer from Rhode Island performing on a bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rialto is the famous bridge across the Grand Canal in Venice.

clue.text: Strange, Keats not in surveillance

indicators.note: strange signals the poet's name is made odd, its letters jumbled

parts.note: someone not in is out

explanation.surface: Oddly, the poet is not at home to the watchers.
explanation.definitionFit: A stakeout is police watching a place covertly, a form of surveillance.
